content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Explain energy changes in terms of bond breaking and making
Use bond energies to calculate enthalpy changes
Explain why bond energy values are averages
is the energy needed to break a specific chemical bond. Understanding bond energies allows us to calculate the energy change for any reaction, even without performing experiments.
The energy required to break one mole of a particular bond in gaseous molecules.
(energy is always needed to break bonds)
$$\Delta H = \text{Energy to break bonds} - \text{Energy released making bonds}$$
Double bonds (=) are stronger than single bonds (-)
Triple bonds (≡) are stronger than double bonds (=)
The exact bond energy depends on the molecular environment.
The mean of bond energies measured in many different molecules.
This is why calculated ΔH values may differ slightly from experimental values.
Explore bond energy calculations — work out the energy change in a reaction using bond energies using the interactive visualisation below.
Draw out the structural formulas showing all bonds
Calculate: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) - Σ(bonds formed)
Calculate the enthalpy change for the combustion of hydrogen:
Bond energies: H-H = 436 kJ/mol, O=O = 498 kJ/mol, O-H = 464 kJ/mol
Bond energies: C-H = 413, Cl-Cl = 243, C-Cl = 346, H-Cl = 432 (all kJ/mol)
Calculate ΔH for the combustion of methane:
Bond energies: C-H = 413, O=O = 498, C=O = 805, O-H = 464 (all kJ/mol)
This is close to the experimental value of -890 kJ/mol. The difference is because bond energies are averages.
The enthalpy change for breaking the N≡N bond is +945 kJ/mol. What does this tell you about the bond?
The N≡N bond has a high bond energy
This means it is a very strong bond
A lot of energy is needed to break it
This is why nitrogen gas (N₂) is so unreactive
The triple bond makes nitrogen very stable
Forgetting to count ALL bonds (including multiple bonds of the same type)
Draw structural formulas and count every single bond
Getting the formula the wrong way around
ΔH = bonds broken - bonds formed (not formed - broken)
Forgetting that bond breaking is endothermic
Breaking bonds absorbs energy; making bonds releases energy
= energy to break one mole of a bond (kJ/mol)
Stronger bonds = higher bond energy (e.g., N≡N = 945 kJ/mol)
Double/triple bonds are stronger than single bonds
